feedback: If a learner predicts 'the heavy side always wins, it can't balance', demonstrate a small mass far out balancing a big mass near the pivot, and point to the two equal moment values.
If a learner places the lighter mass symmetrically (equal distance), ask them to compute F × d for each side and notice the heavier side's larger product.

If a learner measures the lever arm along an angled spanner rather than perpendicular to the line of action, show that only the perpendicular component counts and the along-arm value over-estimates the moment.
Reinforce units: moment is in newton-metres (N·m); a moment is a quantity (force × distance), not a 'turning force'.
Note that equal moments alone do not guarantee equilibrium — an unsupported balanced rule still needs zero resultant force or it can accelerate.
activities.intendedInsight: The turning effect is force × perpendicular distance from the pivot, not force alone; a small force far out balances a large force close in. Balance means equal moments on each side, not equal weights.
learnerActions: Set up a metre-rule on a knife-edge pivot at its own balance point (centre of mass, usually near the 50 cm mark) so the rule's weight has no moment, with slotted masses that can hang at marked distances.
Before adding a lighter mass to balance a heavier mass placed near the pivot, predict WHERE the lighter mass must go and state why in words.
Slide the lighter mass and test; record the force (weight) and perpendicular distance on each side in a data table.
Repeat for several pairs, then check that clockwise moment (F × d) equals anticlockwise moment at balance.
Using an angled spanner on a nut, mark the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action and compare it to the length measured along the arm.
activities.title: Predict-then-measure on a balance beam

feedback: If a learner thinks the jack creates force from nothing, direct attention to the distance each piston moves and the roughly equal work done on both sides.
If a learner confuses force and pressure (e.g. 'the big piston has more pressure'), compute force ÷ area on both sides and show the pressure value is the same while the forces differ.
Reinforce that pressure in a liquid acts in all directions, normal to every surface, and increases with depth — not only downward.

If atmospheric pressure arises, clarify it is the pressure caused by the weight of the air above pressing on surfaces and that it decreases with height/altitude, distinct from the transmitted pressure inside the confined hydraulic fluid.
Reinforce units: pressure in pascals (N/m²).
activities.intendedInsight: Pressure is transmitted equally through a confined fluid (pressure = force ÷ area), so a small force on a small area lifts a large load on a large area — but the multiplied force is paid for in extra distance moved. Nothing comes for free. Atmospheric pressure is the separate everyday pressure of the air column, which decreases with height.
learnerActions: Use a syringe-and-tube hydraulic (small input syringe connected to a large output syringe) or an equivalent two-piston setup.
Predict whether pushing the small piston can lift a heavy load on the large piston, and whether you are 'getting force for free'.

Press the small piston and observe the large piston rise; read or compute the pressure (force ÷ area) on each side and confirm it is approximately equal (friction in real syringes causes small differences).
Track and compare how far the small piston moves versus how far the large piston moves.
State the trade: force is multiplied, but the small piston travels a long way while the big one barely moves, so work in ≈ work out — energy is conserved.
Relate the confined-fluid pressure to atmospheric pressure — the pressure caused by the weight of the air above, acting on all surfaces — and note how atmospheric pressure decreases with height.
activities.title: The hydraulic trade: force up, distance down

feedback: If a learner extends the straight line indefinitely, load the spring past the limit and show the curve and the permanent stretch after unloading.
If a learner treats k as a fixed property of the material only, note that stiffness depends on the spring's dimensions, not just the material.
Reinforce units: stiffness in N/m, read as the gradient of force (N) against extension (m).
Check that k = F/x is computed only within the proportional region, not from a curved part of the graph.
activities.intendedInsight: Extension is directly proportional to applied force up to the limit of proportionality (F = kx), with gradient k being the stiffness; beyond it the graph curves, and past the elastic limit (at or just beyond it) the deformation becomes permanent. Hooke's Law is a special case, not an always-true rule.
learnerActions: Hang slotted masses one at a time on a spring beside a ruler, recording applied force and extension for each load in a table.
Plot force against extension and check that the points fall on a straight line through the origin.
Read the gradient and name it as the stiffness/spring constant k, computing k = F ÷ x for several points to confirm it is constant in the linear region.

Keep loading beyond the linear region; note the point where the straight line bends (the limit of proportionality) and test whether the spring returns to its original length when unloaded (it does not once the elastic limit is passed).

Mark the limit of proportionality (where the line stops being straight) on the graph and state that Hooke's Law holds only up to that point; note that the elastic limit, beyond which the stretch is permanent, is at or just beyond it.
activities.title: Build Hooke's Law from a spring and find the elastic limit

feedback: Treat consolidation tasks as a check on the discovered laws, not as the place to first meet them; if an answer is recognition-only, ask the learner to construct the explanation in their own words.
For the door question, a full answer pushes at the far edge because the larger perpendicular distance gives a larger moment for the same force.
For the jack question, a full answer says force is multiplied but the small piston moves much further, so energy is conserved — not free.
For the spanner question, the longer spanner turns the stiff bolt more easily because its greater perpendicular distance gives a larger moment for the same force.
Illustrations of extension or balance positions are evocative only; rely on the stated values, not on exact drawn lengths.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can state and apply each law, read the law off a graph or diagram, explain the force-for-distance trade shared by levers and hydraulics, and explain the force–extension proportionality of springs, rather than treating them as unrelated formulas.
learnerActions: Place a mass on a drawn or modelled rule to make it balance, justifying the position with F × d on each side.
Complete the relationships in writing: moment = force × perpendicular distance; pressure = force ÷ ___ (area); F = k × ___ (extension).

Sort described situations into 'Hooke's Law holds' versus 'beyond the limit of proportionality', and identify on a given force–extension graph the point where the line stops being straight (the limit of proportionality).
Order a set of springs by stiffness using their force–extension gradients.

Answer the probe questions in writing: where to push a heavy door and why (near the hinge or far edge); whether a hydraulic car jack gives energy for free and what is traded; how to find the spring constant and the elastic limit on a graph; which of a short or long spanner turns a stiff bolt more easily and why.
activities.title: Consolidate and self-check the three laws

feedback: Prompt the learner to state why the line bends at the limit of proportionality, not just that it does.
For the hydraulic diagram, ask the learner to name both the equal pressure and the unequal force and distance, so pressure and force stay distinct.
Note that a fixed diagram names and anchors the parts but does not itself recompute, so pair it with the hands-on or live-model activities where the learner experiences the trade.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct naming of parts — perpendicular distance, equal pressure, elastic limit, pressure acting normal to all surfaces — anchors the vocabulary and pre-empts the perpendicular-distance and force-vs-pressure errors.
learnerActions: Study a labelled balanced-rule diagram and tag the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action on each side.
Study a two-piston hydraulic diagram with equal-pressure arrows and label where force is multiplied and where distance is traded.
Study an annotated force–extension graph: straight line through the origin, gradient k, and the limit of proportionality flagged where the line bends (with the elastic limit at or just beyond it).
Study a pressure-with-depth diagram with arrows acting normal to all surfaces and longer at greater depth.
For each diagram, write the quantity each label represents and the common error it guards against (perpendicular distance vs along-arm; force vs pressure; proportional vs beyond-limit).
activities.title: Reference diagrams for naming and error pre-emption
